method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Primary dysmenorrhoea accounts for about 90% of cases** and **investigations are not routinely required.**
claims.source_text: Primary dysmenorrhoea accounts for approximately 90% of cases … Investigations are not routinely required
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Primary pattern:** pain typically starts 6–12 months after menarche; cramping, intermittent lower abdominal pain starting before or with menses and lasting up to 72 hours.
claims.source_text: Features suggestive of primary dysmenorrhoea Pain typically starting 6-12 months post menarche Cramping, intermittent lower abdominal pain starting prior to or with menses, lasting up to 72 hours
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Atypical features suggesting secondary dysmenorrhoea:** pain worsening towards the end of bleeding · pain from menarche · pain after pelvic infection or features of PID · dysuria or dyschezia during menses · family history of endometriosis · persistent pain despite 3–6 months of adequate empiric treatment.
claims.source_text: Atypical features which are more suggestive of secondary dysmenorrhoea Pain worsening towards the end of bleeding days Pain present from menarche Pain commencing after pelvic infection or features suggestive of pelvic inflammatory disease Dysuria or dyschezia during menses Family history of endometriosis Persistent pain despite an adequate trial of empiric treatment for 3-6 months
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Endometriosis is the most common cause of secondary dysmenorrhoea**; others include obstructive reproductive tract anomalies, adenomyosis, infection including PID, and ovarian cysts.
claims.source_text: Endometriosis (most common cause) Obstructive reproductive tract anomalies Adenomyosis Infection including pelvic inflammatory disease Ovarian cysts
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Consider acute and serious causes of abdominal pain first.**
claims.source_text: Consider acute and serious causes of abdominal pain
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Vaginal examination is rarely indicated in an adolescent**; discuss with a senior clinician, and if needed perform it only once.
claims.source_text: Vaginal examination is rarely indicated in an adolescent. It should be discussed with a senior clinician, and if needed should only be performed once
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider βhCG (with consent)**, especially if sexually active, after unprotected intercourse or with a late/missed period; **consider an STI screen** if features suggest STI or PID.
claims.source_text: Consider ßhCG (with consent) especially if sexually active, unprotected intercourse and/or late/missed period … Consider STI screen if features suggestive of STI or pelvic inflammatory disease
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pelvic ultrasound, usually transabdominal,** for atypical features or no response to an adequate trial of hormonal therapy.
claims.source_text: Pelvic ultrasound, usually transabdominal, should be considered in those with atypical features, or those not responding to an adequate trial of hormonal therapy
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Aim: quality of life** — minimise disruption to school and extra-curricular activities. **First line: NSAIDs and/or hormonal therapy.**
claims.source_text: Management should be focused on quality-of-life improvement, particularly minimising disruption to school attendance and participation in extra-curricular activities … First line medications include NSAIDs and/or hormonal therapies
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Continuous or extended hormonal contraception is recommended over cyclic use.**
claims.source_text: Continuous or extended use of hormonal contraceptives is recommended over cyclic use
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **NSAIDs:** naproxen 5 mg/kg (max 500 mg) BD **or** mefenamic acid 500 mg TDS with food. **Start 1–2 days before menses and continue through the first 2–3 days of bleeding.**
claims.source_text: NSAIDs: Naproxen 5 mg/kg (max 500 mg) BD or Mefenamic acid 500 mg TDS with food … Most effective when started 1--2 days before the onset of menses and continued through the first 2--3 days of bleeding
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Tranexamic acid 1 gram TDS on days of heavy bleeding** — especially useful with concomitant heavy menstrual bleeding.
claims.source_text: Antifibrinolytics: Tranexamic acid 1 gram TDS on days of heavy bleeding … Especially useful in those with concomitant heavy menstrual bleeding
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Non-hormonal medications can be used safely with hormonal ones.** Non-drug therapies can complement medicines, or replace them if medicines are unsuitable or unacceptable.
claims.source_text: Can be safely used with hormonal medications … Non-pharmacological therapies can be used to complement medical therapies or as an alternative if medications are unsuitable/unacceptable
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Combined oral contraceptive pill:** if pain is not adequately reduced, use it continuously (skip hormone-free tablets); check contraindications. Examples: levonorgestrel 150 microg/ethinylestradiol 30 microg (Levlen) daily, or norethisterone 0.5 mg/ethinylestradiol 35 mcg (Norimin) daily.
claims.source_text: Combined oral contraceptive pill If inadequate reduction in pain with standard use, continuous use is recommended (i.e. avoiding hormone free tablets) See Contraindications Levonorgestrel 150 microg/ethinyl estradiol 30 microg (Levlen®) daily Norethisterone 0.5 mg, ethinylestradiol 35 mcg (Norimin ®) daily
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Oral progestogen if oestrogen is contraindicated** (no increased VTE risk): norethisterone (Primolut N) starting at 5 mg BD, continuously.
claims.source_text: Oral progestogen Useful if oestrogen is contraindicated No increased risk of venous thromboembolism Norethisterone (Primolut N®) starting at 5 mg BD, continuously
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Etonogestrel implant (Implanon), 3-yearly:** may reduce pain and blood loss; 20% become amenorrhoeic.
claims.source_text: Subdermal progestogen May reduce menstrual pain and blood loss 20% of users become amenorrheic Etonogestrel implant (Implanon®), 3 yearly
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Levonorgestrel IUD (Mirena or Kyleena), 5–8-yearly:** reduces blood loss and pain; safe post-menarche regardless of age; **in adolescents usually inserted under anaesthetic.**
claims.source_text: Progestogen-releasing intrauterine device (IUD) Reduces blood loss and menstrual pain 20% of users become amenorrheic Can be safely used post-menarche regardless of age Usually involves insertion under anaesthetic in adolescents Levonorgestrel IUD (Mirena®or Kyleena), 5-8 yearly
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Review 3 months after starting treatment**; sooner if side effects are unacceptable.
claims.source_text: 3 months after treatment to assess efficacy … Earlier review may be required if unacceptable or intolerable side effects are present
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Refer to gynaecology** for suspected secondary dysmenorrhoea, atypical features, or pain not responding to first-line treatment — including **persistent pain despite at least 3–6 months of adequate empiric treatment.**
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with gynaecology team when Suspicion of secondary dysmenorrhoea Atypical features Pain not responding adequately to first line treatment … refer to local gynaecology service for further assessment if there are atypical features or persistent pain despite an adequate trial of empiric treatment for at least 3-6 months
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discharge once management has started and a clear follow-up plan is made.**
claims.source_text: Consider discharge when Management initiated and clear plan for follow up made
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Dysmenorrhoea' (Last updated October 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Dysmenorrhoea/, retrieved 2026-09-23
